speechtext:
I will deal with that because the agreement with Ontario is not complete. It does not include succession duties. It was limited.
There is one other fiction that has a bearing in this debate with which I wish to deal and deal explicitly. It is the fiction that no pressure has been applied by the dominion government on the provinces. That is so far from the facts as to bear no resemblance to them.
I have pointed out in the first place the inadequacy of any field left to any nonsigning province without imposing on its taxpayers burdens that, in addition to the existing federal impositions, would be too heavy to be borne. In the second place, there has been that obstinate refusal on the part of the federal government to collect provincial income tax for any provincial government which seeks to collect its own personal tax or its own tax on corporations. It has compelled any such government to set up its own expensive collecting machinery. In the third place, the federal government has tried to make these agreements as attractive as possible to any province in the hope that all will sign. But, Mr. Speaker, there is more direct evidence than that of pressure on the part of the federal government. One has only to recall the statements made by the ministers who signed the agreement on behalf of the Alberta government a few years ago when remarks were made on the part of these ministers that a pistol had been held to their heads and they were signing the agreement virtually at pistol point.
This afternoon the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Breton) had a good deal to say about the fact that the premier of the province of Ontario had signed an agreement in October, 1952. Evidently he has completely overlooked what the premier of Ontario had to say about the agreement that he signed at that time, for here are the words that were uttered by the premier of Ontario on October 21, 1952. He said that at best the agreement was nothing more than a "stopgap arrangement." He warned that it did not provide a solution to the municipal problem, which in turn is "dependent on a shift of taxes and revenue from dominion sources to the province and then to the municipalities". These next words are a direct quotation from his remarks:
We have urged the dominion government to begin discussions with the provinces to obtain these objectives. The present tax system is outmoded.

These are the words of the premier of Ontario and he has made similar statements since that are to the same effect as the remarks he made at that time.
Nothing short of a dominion-provincial conference seeking agreement with reference to fields of taxation will be adequate to meet the needs of the situation. The provinces of Canada have important constitutional rights and responsibilities. Those rights and responsibilities must be respected. In Canada we live under a federal system. There never would have been a Canada had there not been a federal system and, sir, the responsibilities which the provinces and their creatures, the municipalities, are bearing today are becoming ever more costly. While that process has been continuing, while their burdens have been growing, the federal government on the other hand has in fact been increasing its powers under our constitution by the extent to which it has been centralizing at Ottawa the collection of revenues. Sir, prior to the war the percentage of the total taxes in Canada collected by the federal government was 39 per cent. Last year that percentage had doubled to 78 per cent. More federal taxation and expenditure mean more federal power at the expense of the provinces.
Warnings like those that came from the eloquent tongue of the late Angus Macdonald have fallen on deaf ears opposite, so that today we have confronting Canada a situation which is the inevitable result of the policies followed by the federal government and its failure to seek agreement with all the provinces through the medium of a dominion-provincial conference.
This situation, Mr. Speaker, is a matter of concern, not simply to the province of Quebec, not simply to Quebec members in this house, but to all of Canada, because we see here, and have seen it in this debate, the wells of Canadian unity being poisoned by the statements that have been made by hon. members opposite; bellicose statements exposing the same kind of belligerent truculent attitude that was shown by the Minister of Finance during the course of his remarks in the budget debate.
It is imperative that there be called a dominion-provincial conference. Only the Prime Minister of Canada can call a dominion-provincial conference. The agenda for that conference must include this whole field of taxing powers and responsibilities. It must take due account of the necessity of honouring and respecting, both in the letter and in the spirit, all existing agreements. It must seek in the long run, under the proper auspices and with a patriotic Canadian spirit, to secure a better deal than any of the provinces have 83276-266
The Budget-Mr. Fleming had as yet. It would mean an end, Mr. Speaker, to a situation such as that which now has arisen and for which this federal government must accept responsibility.
No one in this house has spoken more eloquently on the subject of national unity than has the Prime Minister, and upon the necessity for maintaining that unity. Today national unity in Canada is threatened by this situation that has been allowed by the federal government to emerge. Provocative truculence on the part of ministers and members opposite is no contribution to the settlement of this problem. What has been exhibited here on the part of the federal government is evidently a determination to beat the province of Quebec to its knees.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, it was a strange afterthought, it was a remark completely out of tone with the other remarks made by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech, when he said at the end of his remarks that the door was still open. It was a curious afterthought, and completely different from the prevailing tone of the minister's remarks in relation to this subject in his budget speech. It is evident that if there is to be any discussion, so far as the attitude of the government opposite has been expressed, the Quebec government will have to come cap in hand and rap on the door of the Minister of Finance.
I say this is a matter of concern to all of Canada. The fact is that all the provinces have asked for a resumption of the dominion-provincial conference. When it adjourned in 1950 it did not end there. It adjourned, ostensibly to meet later, with optimistic statements on the part of the Prime Minister and other representatives of the federal government; optimistic statements about the good that had been accomplished by the conference and what was yet to be accomplished in the course of further discussion.
Is it not a strange contradiction, is it not an amazing commentary on the attitude of the government opposite, that at this very moment at Geneva representatives of the Canadian government are sitting around a table with representatives of communist governments, Russia and China, to discuss matters of at least common concern, yet the Canadian government will not bring itself to sit down with fellow Canadians representative of the provinces to discuss matters of common concern?
It is not long ago that the Prime Minister returned from a tour abroad during which he visited several of our sister nations of the commonwealth. He undertook this tour with the complete approbation, and indeed the earnest good will of all political parties in this house.

The Budget*-Mr. Pickersgill
During the course of the tour the Prime Minister gave expression, as indeed we all knew he would, in his visits to other countries, both those in the commonwealth and those outside the commonwealth, to the Canadian spirit of friendliness, conciliation and good will. This same spirit is urgently needed now here. It rests with the Prime Minister of Canada and no one else to decide whether a dispute, which has already been the occasion of very bitter expressions on the part of some hon. members opposite, a dispute which apparently is becoming more bitter day by day if we are to judge by their bitterness, is to be permitted to continue to become more divisive, more threatening to Canadian unity, or whether instead there is to be a sensible approach in the true Canadian spirit of good will and understanding. Which course is to be followed, bitterness, disunity and division, or the conference table, the spirit of good will, understanding and accord? The choice rests with the Prime Minister of Canada.

This is a curious remark
from the hon. member. I suppose he is not unfamiliar with a reference book prepared in 1945 for the dominion-provincial conference on reconstruction, the so-called green book, bearing the label "Personal Income Taxes." It is a federal publication, so perhaps he even had something to do with compiling it. The province of Quebec first levied a tax on income in 1939 (chap. 16, Laws of 1940). It differed from the tax of the other provinces in that it imposed a flat levy of 15 per cent on the amount of tax payable by an individual to the dominion . . .
I draw to the attention of the minister the fact that this tax was first imposed in 1939. I think he is dealing with the statutory reference of 1940. There may have been a change made then, but I am prepared to go by what the federal government said in its green book.
But, Mr. Speaker, be that as it may, whether it began in 1940 or 1939, it had been in existence for not less than two years before the dominion-provincial agreement of 1942. And I also draw to the attention of the hon. member the fact that the rate then in


effect in the province of Quebec was 15 per cent of the amount of taxation payable by an individual to the dominion-the same rate now proposed. The federal government in those days was generous enough and big enough to collect that tax on behalf of the province.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of following what has been said in the last while by hon. members who have preceded me in the debate in the discussion of a number of very interesting subjects. We have heard many speeches on dominion-provincial relations; and earlier today we heard from the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) an interesting address on the subject of Social Credit. Let me say at once that I always enjoy his exposition of the subject. Each time I hear it I have the hope that I will understand the theory. Yesterday evening I think he came about as close to disclosing the philosophy as he ever did when he mentioned that it had been referred to as scrip tease. I thought that at last he was getting down to the bare facts of Social Credit. But it was not to be.
What I have to say will not follow along the lines of the debate which has been taking place this afternoon. I would like to speak directly to what is in the budget speech, particularly as it affects trade. In my opinion this budget overlooks a great many

things which the people of Canada had a right to expect to find in it. My understanding is that a budget should do three things: It is a review of the current economic position of Canada; it is an announcement of the fiscal and other changes to be recommended by the government; and it is also a forecast of government policy. Under those three headings I should like to examine the provisions in the budget and see to what extent they are satisfactory.
First of all, in giving a review of the economic situation in Canada I believe the Minister of Finance tried to give a rather optimistic picture. However in one or two places in his speech he had to admit-and I shall quote his own words

that the situation is not as rosy as he would like to have us believe. For example, as reported at page 3725 of Hansard for April 6, he made this significant statement when he referred to the fact that there has been a slowing down of business activity and a drop in incomes in certain sectors of our country. He gave this as the reason:
This slowing down in the growth of defence expenditures no doubt contributed to the levelling off of production in some industries that became evident toward the end of 1953.
That is a significant statement, for this reason, that at various times the public has been led to believe that it has been the general economic policy of this government and of the party which now holds power that has been responsible for that condition in Canada described as prosperity. But now we have the significant statement that due to a lower expenditure on defence, immediately there has been a slowing down of production, a levelling off of prices, and so on.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In some industries.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, in some industries; and later on I shall point out the industries concerned. The significant point is that we are told all these conferences that are being held throughout the world, including the one in progress today, are designed to bring about a peaceful situation in the world, a situation in which all nations can continue to live in peace and prosperity. I believe all nations are looking forward to a time when war will become unnecessary.
If that is the over-all objective, then we must dare to hope that defence expenditures will be reduced as a regular thing in the future. If the small drop in national defence expenditures in Canada this year has already affected our economy to the extent indicated by the Minister of Finance, then surely it is time to do some serious thinking as to what the effect will be if conditions were such that it was possible for us in Canada as well as for 83276-266J
The Budget-Mr. Zaplitny people in the United States and in other countries to cut defence expenditures in half, or to even less than that. Surely that is a matter which must be given serious consideration. Because until the beginning of the second world war we had a situation in Canada which was described in various terms, but was commonly known as a depression. During those times there were members in the house who suggested to the government that it was not necessary, in a country as wealthy as Canada in potential natural resources, to have unemployment and to have poverty in the midst of plenty. Those suggestions and ideas were disregarded. In fact I well remember that Mr. Dunning, who was minister of finance in those days, used quite often to brush aside such suggestions with the question, "Where is the money to come from?"
Later on as we moved along it was discovered that money was the least important of the considerations, and that as long as we had the natural resources and the potential, a medium of exchange could be found. And it was found. We found we could expand the economy and the industry of this country to an extent undreamed of in 1939. Those who would have said that it was possible in, let us say, 1938 or 1939 to expand the production and industrial potential capacity of the country to the extent it was expanded in, let us say, 1945, would have been called, and indeed were called, dreamers and visionaries. Yet they spoke the economic truth.
I wish to refer to another statement in the minister's speech, found on the very next page, where he said:
There is no need for me to go into detail concerning the nature of the present economic situation. It is characterized by more unemployment than we had last year at this same time, and by more unemployment than any of us like to see. It is marked also by a slackening in the growth of production and by declines in certain industries.
There is an indication of the fact that we are slowly, perhaps not too slowly, drifting back into a position of recession which may end up in a major depression. The reason I put that on the record is that the paragraph farther down, as far as I can see after reading the speech, is the only recommendation the minister had to make as to what could be done about such a position. Here are his words, as reported at page 3726 of Hansard:
The re-emergence of keen competition in trade means readjustment and reappraisal. It means a sharpening of pencils and a careful re-examination of managerial and labour efficiency. This is not an easy process, but it is a very necessary one, and the longer it is postponed the more difficult it becomes.
So far as I can see, that was the advice the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) had for those industries who find themselves in a.

The Budget-Mr. Zaplitny depressed position. He advised them to sharpen their pencils, to look into their methods of doing business, to create greater efficiency and so forth. May I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that that is not the solution. I do not believe that anyone in this house seriously believes that that is the solution. It is not a matter of greater or more efficient production. When we look over the situation in Canada and when we listen to the speeches of private members on the government side of the house, we hear from day to day that their greatest problem is in the field of marketing. We have surpluses of this and of that; we have produced and are producing great quantities. It is not a matter of being able to produce more; it is not a matter of greater efficiency. It is a matter of creating, in my opinion, a proper price relationship in order that the medium of exchange may be as equally distributed as it is possible in our economic set-up so that the wheels of industry may continue to turn.
I now come to some of the budgetary changes. I do not need to go into detail. They are available to the public and printed in the press. It strikes me as rather strange when I look at the changes that were made, -and I am in favour of some of them; for example, the reduction or the removal of the sales tax on implements or equipment used by municipalities, the reduction of excise taxes on certain goods, are desirable- when you boil it all down, when you study all the budgetary changes you find that it all amounts to so little that the general public has expressed a great deal of dissatisfaction and discontent.
Only a short time ago, in the budget before the election, it struck me, as I went back over the literature published by the Liberal party during the election, they took a great deal of credit for what they called the "sunshine budget". They took a great deal of pride in some of the tax reductions that were made. They made it appear as though they were well on the way to lifting some of the tax burden from those who now have to bear it. Since the election is over we seem to come right back again, to the budget which was brought down this year and which I think was correctly described by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) as a scrawny budget. It has been described in various terms. I find in one of the newspapers that the secretary-treasurer of the Canadian Congress of Labour characterized it as an empty budget. He was not far out. They also point out that the government seems to have ignored almost completely the representations made by agriculture.


I am not going to go through that, but to illustrate I hold in my hand a letter and certain other representations made by the Manitoba Federation of Agriculture and Cooperation. This is an organization which represents a large number of farmers. It also represents the co-operative movement in Manitoba. I have found them to be extremely modest in their requests, and so has the government. We are informed that this organization made a certain request to the government with respect to certain tariff changes. To give an illustration of the way they feel about it I shall read the first two paragraphs of this letter. It starts out by saying:
On March 9, 1954. in a memorandum presented to the Minister of Finance, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, of which this organization is a member body, requested that certain changes be made in the Customs Tariff and the Excise Tax Act.
In bringing down his budget on April 6, the Hon. D. C. Abbott made no reference to the suggestions of the federation of agriculture and made none of the suggested changes in the Customs Tariff or Excise Tax Act. This is a regrettable omission.
To that I say, hear, hear. In a moment I shall make reference to some of the requests that have been heard. Those requests were exceedingly modest and reasonable and I dare to hope that the government will yet take the opportunity, which will be present when we are in committee, to recommend certain amendments to the resolutions which will be before us and make those changes.
The federation asked that all instruments of production used by farmers in Canada be duty free. Certainly there was nothing very radical about that request nor anything very unreasonable about it. It is in line with what the government says is their policy. We have been repeatedly told that they believe in lower tariffs; that they do not believe that farm implements, which enter into the cost of production, should be subject to customs duty. But there are a number of very important pieces of equipment, let us say, which are used in farming which are still subject to taxes, and this organization asked that they be removed. Nothing was done about it, and no mention was even made of that request in the budget speech.
They also asked that the sales tax on stock feeds be removed, and that apparently was not done. One or two other requests were made which I hope the government will still be prepared to carry out before the resolutions are carried.
What about government policy? I believe that is the most important part of the budget, Mr. Speaker. Apparently what budgetary changes the minister has recommended the

government feels are sufficient. We may have a difference of opinion on that, but we are not going to be able to do very much about it. Government policy is important because it has to do with the future. And in a country as young as Canada I believe we must have a policy, and a great deal will depend on the type of government policy that is in operation in future years. I find that the government has actually no policy for the future. I say that because in 1949 the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) made a certain statement as to what the philosophy of the government was and that was quoted as recently as March 9 by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), apparently with approval. These are the words:
Canada is a free enterprise economy and the initiative for economic expansion rests with private individuals and firms. The government will endeavour, through its policies, to create a climate within which private initiative thrives and industrial expansion is encouraged.
There is nothing particularly wrong with that statement except for the fact that when you analyse it it means that the government is prepared to do nothing in the way of economic planning, believing as they do in what they call free enterprise, which sometimes is referred to as private enterprise. Call it what you will, they believe in the policy of laissez-faire, drift. I take issue with that policy because I believe we are in a time in which, whether this government likes it or not, whether any party in this house likes it or not, the government of Canada is going to have to take a greater share in the economic affairs of the country if they are to fulfil their responsibilities.
We have advocated and do advocate economic planning. There are those who oppose it. Well, let us face the issue. Let us give each other the benefit of the doubt. We are honest about our opinions. We believe in economic planning because we believe that there is nothing that can be substantially accomplished without planning. That is being proved every day in our business and industrial affairs. It does make a difference what the planning is for and it makes a difference who is doing the planning, but if the government actually believes that they are going to take some responsibility for the general welfare and the economic development of the country they must accept that the philosophy of economic planning is necessary.
After examining the proposals of the budget and the budget speech we have heard questions asked everywhere on certain points. I am sure hon. members who were home recently during the Easter recess have had these questions thrown at them regardless of
The Budget-Mr. Zaplitny the constituency they represent or the party to which they belong. People are asking what is being done about unemployment. What are we going to say? Are we to quote for them the words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce which apparently is government policy? He stated that it is private initiative which must look after the economic affairs of this country, and that the government takes no responsibility for these matters. Are these the answers we are supposed to give the unemployed? If we are to follow out the government policy and interpret it in that way then certainly the people in this country will wonder what we are doing.
We are asked about the grain situation. Recently figures have been presented in the press showing that over one billion bushels of grain are now available in Canada. We will soon be entering into another crop year. In 1954 the acreage under seed will be as high as ever and it is estimated we will have another huge crop for this year. But then, if we get a good crop, as good as we have had in past years, what will the situation be? How are we going to turn that grain into cash? I agree, to some extent, with what the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has often said, namely, that a large amount of grain in storage on the farms or in the grain elevators is not a bad thing. Of course, I believe we might well have lean years as well as the more productive years we have had, and the situation may well arise when we may be very happy if we have a great deal of grain in storage because it is one of the best, and least perishable foods on this earth. But the farmer has to pay his expenses, pay for his tractor fuel, hired help, and all the other incidental expenses which go into farming, as the Minister of Agriculture very well knows. To the farmer grain stored in the granary or in the elevator, unless he can turn it into cash, is not a very useful commodity. Therefore, something has to be done to turn that into cash. Various suggestions have been made but none of them apparently have met with the approval of the government, though it is a matter which is becoming more and more urgent, particularly since we are approaching next year's crop.
We have been told by the Minister of Trade and Commerce that the best we can hope for is a quota of seven bushels per acre during the present crop year. But what will the situation be after that? On the first of August it is more than likely to be down to two bushels an acre again and how will farmers handle that situation when they have some 1952 crop, when they have not sold the 1953 crop and the 1954 crop is coming on top of that? How are they going to meet their expenses? How are they going to safeguard

The Budget-Mr. Zaplitny their credit which is even now in jeopardy? And how are the dealers and local merchants going to continue to carry their customers with the credit they have been extending, unless some of that grain, or a substantial part of that grain can be turned into cash? That situation has to be faced and faced very quickly, but apparently so far the government has no plan and has given us no hope that they have any solution to the problem.
The government has turned down all the suggestions that have been made. The budget debate has not brought out any new suggestions, nor have any alternative suggestions been advanced by the government. We are anxious to know what they are going to do about that situation.
Then there is the question of price relationship. I am not going to speak extensively on that subject this evening because I have spoken so often on the question of prices in this house that I hesitate to weary hon. members any longer. But I feel strongly about this because I believe a great many of our troubles can be traced to the price policies of the present administration. I believe it was a major mistake when in 1946, 1947 and 1948 the government began to abolish price controls as quickly as possible and permitted the condition to be created where price relationship went entirely out of joint.
The government, of course, will probably say this is a matter which can be handled quite properly within the provinces. I am not going to go into that controversy because we have heard enough about dominion-provincial disputes during this debate. But I would like to say this, that no one can seriously claim that any provincial government in this country could successfully operate a price control system within its own borders. It is either a question of this parliament enacting the proper legislation or we will not have it at all. Let us get that point quite clearly fixed. But in speaking of price control, and I have mentioned this point before, I hope it will be clearly understood that I do not necessarily mean lower prices. As a matter of fact, it does not have to mean lower prices at all. It would mean the establishing of a price relationship so that the cost of production can be safeguarded in relation to the price at which the product is sold.
At this point I would like to refer once again to the speech of the Minister of Finance and point out that what this government has done is to permit 50 per cent of the savings and of the incomes of those who are on pensions to be confiscated by inflation. I make that statement on the authority of the Minister of Finance himself, although, of course,


he did not say so in so many words. However, if you turn to the appendix to the budget, at page 3759 you will find a graph which sets out the gross national expenditure and underneath that there is written "in current and constant dollars." Now the current line on this graph shows $24 billion and the dollar, taking 1935 to 1939 as a basis of 100, drops down to exactly one-half. In other words, this is an admission by the Department of Finance that the dollar of 1935 to 1939 is today worth exactly 50 cents. It means that those whose income has not increased since price controls were removed, and who are for example on a pension or a war veterans allowance, or some other fixed income, have had one-half of their income confiscated by inflation.
Now that is a fact which the government cannot dispute, and that has also been the effect on those who have saved up a little money during the years of the war or previous to that, or who retired during 1945 and 1946 as many people did. They are mostly farmers and business people and others who have saved up a little money, put it in the bank, and hoped that that money would see them through. They have found that inflation has confiscated 50 cents of every dollar they saved. That is also true of people who bought war bonds with dollars which were worth 100 cents. When they receive their money, or when these bonds are redeemed, they are going to get dollars which are now worth 50 cents.
That is confiscation and it is a strange irony to find that the same party which so often used to accuse the C.C.F. of the intention of confiscating the people's money through nationalization of the banks- though that is a form of propaganda I do not hear any more-themselves today stand guilty of having confiscated 50 per cent of the savings of the Canadian people and of all those who are on a fixed income such as a pension.
That is what has happened under our price relationships since price controls were taken off; and that is not all of it. We have a marketing problem. We were told by the Minister of Agriculture not so long ago that there would be no difficulty in selling Canadian farm products on the overseas market provided we are prepared to accept the price that they are willing to pay. That statement in itself may be a perfectly truthful one, and I am not disputing it; but what does it mean? It means that Canadian producers, whether they be producers of grain, livestock or any other farm commodity, would have to accept, in many instances, a price which would be less than or very close

to the cost of production. In other words, they would have to accept a price at which they could not economically operate their farms. If we had a proper system of price relationships, where the costs of production could be safeguarded by keeping at the proper level the price of things that go into the cost of production such as fuel, farm machinery and all the other things that go into farm production, it would be possible for Canadian farmers today to accept a lower price than that which they are currently asking or getting and to retain those world markets which have slipped through our fingers in recent years. But certainly no one today can be heard to say, "Oh, yes, we have allowed your cost of production to go up until it is almost double what it was a few years ago, but if you are willing to sell your production at half the price you are now getting, we will find markets for it." We have got ourselves into that dilemma owing to the fact that there is no proper price relationship between the cost of production and the price of the goods we sell.
Then what about social security? I have already pointed out that inflation has reduced the real income of those who are on pensions, who draw family allowances and so on. People are asking what this parliament is prepared to do about increasing family allowances, old age pensions, blind pensions and so on, in order at least to compensate them for the loss they have sustained due to inflation. After looking through the budget and listening to the speeches made so far by those on the government side of the house, I can offer no hope to those who ask these questions. Apparently nothing is to be proposed to this house this session with the exception, of course, of legislation which we expect in respect to persons who are disabled.
When we plead for improvements in our social security measures we are often admonished by members on the other side of the house, including members of the cabinet, *-even the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) himself-who point out that it is going to cost money to do these things. Obviously it will cost money. But, Mr. Speaker, I plead on behalf of the aged, the disabled, the blind and so on and I do so without any apology because I ask for them no greater generosity than that which the government has seen fit to lavish upon the members of this house and the members of the Senate. There seemed to be no hesitation with regard to where the money was coming from in that respect.
Then what about a national health plan? Obviously that is another one of those skeletons in the closet which the government
The Budget-Mr. Zaplitny hopes will not rattle too loudly and will not attract too much attention. They hope that they can tiptoe past that issue quietly without having it raised too many times during this session. But it is another one of those election promises which have been made again and again. No doubt it will be made just as blithely at the next election as it has been in the past. I think it is time to play fair and to be honest with the Canadian public. If this government intends to bring in a national health plan, then certainly something should be done in this session to indicate that it is going to be done before this parliament is dissolved.
I have already pointed out that we believe in economic planning and in establishing a proper price relationship. May I just say now in a general way that I believe it is time we had a new economic philosophy, a new way of looking at things. Here I speak for myself only as an individual, and I say that I believe it is time we accepted the philosophy of co-operation in place of the philosophy of competition. I know that a large majority of the members of this house think that the competitive system is the right type of economic system. I respect their views, but to me it runs counter to all the other teachings and to all the other things which we accept as being right on the moral side of life. From the time we learn to speak or start in to school or take part in any activities in relation to our fellow human beings, we are taught to respect each other and to help each other.
For example, we are taught the golden rule: Do unto others as you would have them do unto you. But as soon as we get into the economic sphere, as soon as we get to the age where we must make a living, then we have to pervert and degrade the golden rule. In order to live with the system you have to do others before they do you. There is something fundamentally wrong about that concept. There is a conflict between the moral forces which we accept and boast about as the Christian principles of kindness and brotherly love. Then we turn around in our economic affairs and we attempt to live in a cutthroat or jungle fashion: we compete and fight. Often I used to thrill to a statement made by the former prime minister of Canada. I used to love to hear one phrase he used so often during the years of war, when he said that we must have a new social order in which human need will be the cardinal principle and not human greed. How little of that philosophy one finds in this budget or in the policies of the present government.

The Budget-Mr. Zaplitny
I believe it is time that we accepted the philosophy of co-operation, of helping each other in our activities, and translated that philosophy into our economic system. It is not something that is going to be done overnight. I am not so optimistic or so idealistic as to think that. But I think it is time a good start were made. If we accept that philosophy seriously and want to translate it into our economic affairs, the place to do it is in our annual budget in order to show that we believe in helping each other instead of competing with each other.
There are business people today who are beginning to realize that this whole question of competition, which to them has been sold as the idea of free enterprise, is not what they thought it was in the first place. From time to time we get reports on the growth of monopolies, combines and cartels, these economic machines which try to throttle free competition, which try to put the small man out of business in order that the big monopoly can operate more freely. All these things are beginning to persuade the people that more co-operation in economic life is needed in order to bring it into line with the philosophy of co-operation that we accept in our moral principles.
In addition to that I will say only this. I think it is time that this parliament was prepared to raise its sights. This budget which we are now discussing is not something we can feel proud of. Somehow, I think every one of us should have a slightly guilty feeling; and those who are directly responsible must, of course, bear the greatest portion of it. When we leave this parliament, when this session is completed, and go back into the constituencies, people will say to us, "So you have passed the budget; you have made provision for certain taxation and so on"; and they will ask, "What have you done that is new? What economic plan have you developed that is going to solve our unemployment situation or is going to do something about trade, or about our grain problem?" and so on.
We are going to have to say that the excise tax on jewelry, fur coats, cameras and fishing rods was reduced. I am sure there will be great comfort in that for the half a million unemployed who are wondering how they are going to pay their rent or make the next payment on their house or car. With the finance company looking over their shoulders and breathing down their necks, it will be a great comfort to them to be told that they are going to be able to buy cameras, fishing rods, jewelry or fur coats a little more cheaply than before. I am sure these are not the kind


of things in which these people are interested. I think it is time that we raised our sights and realized the great development potential there is in this country, particularly in the northern areas. We should be prepared to accept public investment as one of the methods to bring about that development.
I am not opposed to private investment but there are times and places where, because of the nature of things, this great potential will remain undeveloped unless public investment is used as an instrument of development. The whole history of Canada proves that, and I need not go into it in detail. I believe it is time that we were prepared to set up an investment board which would have a twofold function. One function would be to provide a place where the public could invest their surplus funds and the other would be to direct investment toward the useful development of our natural resources. I believe we have a great deal of potential wealth and unless we are prepared to remain hewers of wood and carriers of water for United States capital we must be prepared to use Canadian capital and public investment where necessary in order to develop the great potentialities of our country.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I see it, it is the wish of every member of the house that oratory be spared so that the present debate on the budget may be as short and as concise as possible. In accordance with this wish and to help the advance toward a successful early end of the session, I will circumscribe my remarks to a few points of special interest to my own constituents and deal mainly with a proposed amendment to the Income Tax Act with respect to mutual insurance companies, with federal-provincial relations and with two or three other points arising from the impressive speech delivered by our able Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) on the night of April 6 last. May I be permitted first to extend my sincere congratulations, and those of the population of Glengarry-Prescott, to the minister for his comprehensive review of Canada's economic and financial position. His conclusions on our national production in 1953 and his forecast for 1954 are not only most encouraging but contain a factual indication of the ascending development of our country under a competent Liberal administration.
By many sources, including stout supporters of the opposition, it has been said that the Minister of Finance has presented a "wait and see" budget. Never, perhaps, was a more impressive tribute paid to a government financial expert. By saying so, even those who intended to criticize were recognizing the far-reaching viewpoints that

obtained in the preparation of the budget by the Minister of Finance. His realistic approach to all economic and financial problems made him realize that the world, and consequently Canada, had reached a turning point where careful steps alone are to be made if one wants his country to go ahead in the international financial organization without disrupting our own industrial or commercial set-up. For all this, and the tactful way in which he managed to protect so many sectors of the population from being hurt by an unfair distribution of taxes among the paying public, the Minister of Finance is to be thanked and congratulated.
But, in opening my remarks, I indicated that I intended to speak briefly about a subject that is of particular interest to my constituents, that of a proposed amendment to the Income Tax Act with reference to mutual insurance companies. On this, which is also of great interest to the great majority of Canadian farmers, I wish to express my fear as to the consequences of the budget income tax resolution No. 6 which reads as follows:
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Income Tax Act and to provide, amongst other things:
6.	For the taxation of a resident mutual insurance corporation, ... as though the surplus arising from its insurance activities on and after January 1, 1954, were a profit from a business, and declaring that a non-resident mutual insurance corporation, other than a life insurance corporation, shall be deemed to be and always to have been subject to taxation on that basis.
This resolution might have to be clarified, but I am given to understand that it would allow the government to re-establish as taxable the surpluses of mutual insurance companies, thus disregarding the favourable report of the royal commission which gave its opinion that purely mutual companies should be taxed only on investment income. As you know, Mr. Speaker, this opinion was concurred in by the income tax appeal board and backed up by the Supreme Court of Canada last summer.
If that is the meaning of resolution No. 6 as it stands, I want immediately to take a firm stand against it and to ask hon. members of this house to keep in mind the danger involved when the resolution is discussed in further detail by the house. The great majority of farmers of my constituency have their fire insurance with the Glengarry Farmers' Mutual Fire Insurance Company or with the Prescott Farmers' Mutual Fire Insurance Company. The two insurance companies are giving insurance protection at cost and any surplus they build up is solely for the reserve demanded by the department of insurance. There are no profits.
There is no doubt, if these two companies have to pay extra taxes along the suggested lines, that the additional cost would have to 83276-267
The Budget-Mr. Bruneau be charged to the insured farmers who, in my estimation, are already charged heavily enough. What is bound to happen in Glen-garry-Prescott can be multiplied across the country by the number of constituencies where farmers are organized on a mutual basis for fire insurance protection. That is why I think that it would be in the general interest that the members of the house, especially those representing rural constituencies, should scrutinize resolution No. 6 when the amending bill is before the house.
I also indicated in my preliminary remarks that I intended to speak about federal-provincial financial relations. On this subject as well I will be brief, but I think, at this stage of the debate, that it is about time that the voice of a French-speaking Canadian living outside of the province of Quebec should be heard, pointing out the importance of standing united as citizens of a great and fastgrowing country. The only direct reference I will make to the statement of the Minister of Finance on the matter will be to say that the vast majority of my constituents entirely agree with his understanding of the constitutional rights on taxation.
(Translation):
It would not be right for me to continue my remarks on that subject without congratulating most sincerely the hon. Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Lesage) on the outstandingly clear presentation he made of this matter in the afternoon of April 14. He really did examine the problem in its true light, setting it out in a perfectly sober and logical fashion, throwing back the responsibility for double taxation on the shoulders of those to whom it really belongs, that is, on those members of the Quebec legislature who have voted this provincial income tax legislation. The minister was fully qualified to speak on behalf of his Quebec colleagues. Speaking for myself, and with due regard to my very inadequate qualifications, I would make so bold as to express the opinion of those who have been called, in the province of Quebec, the "separated brethren", and for the survival of whom, we are told, some are prepared to fight to the bitter end.
(Text):
As a representative of a merged constituency where the best elements of the two great racial groups of Canada are represented, I feel particularly well qualified to speak on that subject. A good number of my constituents are, as I am, of French extraction and speak that language. They are consequently very interested in any political moves that are made in their name across the Quebec border. The English-speaking

The Budget-Mr. Bruneau group also has a keen interest in these moves lor they may have, as in this case of double taxation, a devastating effect on national unity and on the whole ol the Canadian economy.
But what prompted me mainly to say a lew words on this question today is the fact that most of the steps taken in Quebec for the so-called protection of provincial autonomy are represented as being moved for the defence of the rights and the survival of French Canadians, no matter where they live in Canada. The latest instance along this line was the adoption by the Quebec government of the act to create a new provincial income tax. I wish to state emphatically today that French-speaking Canadians living outside of the province of Quebec do not agree with this interpretation.
As citizens of Canada we are fully conscious that everything tending to disrupt efforts for unity is not in our best interests. We feel that the Quebec income tax law tends only to separate Quebec from the government of this country, instead of putting forward an authentic desire for co-operation that would give monetary help to the taxpayers of Quebec as well as solidify the national structure without endangering the constitutional rights of the French-speaking population.
As "separate brothers", we cannot accept the contention of the Quebec administrator that the British North America Act was a pact between the two main races of Canada. We consider it, as the fathers of confederation considered it at the time, an act uniting the provinces of one country under a single government charged with the general administration and with full powers of taxation, leaving to the provinces questions of local administration with powers restricted to direct taxation. If the British North America Act were a pact between races, how would the Quebec government be able to legally act for the French-speaking population living in other provinces?
On the other hand, as has been said so well by others who have taken part in this debate, no one questions the right of the provinces to direct taxation. But if the British North America Act limits the taxing powers of the provinces to direct taxation, it does not mean that this limitation gives them a priority in that field as the Quebec administrator would like us to believe. It does not mean either that the fathers of confederation were logical in granting equal powers in the same field of taxation to both the provinces and the federal government. But it is our feeling that we should try to make the best of what we have as long as the fiscal clauses of the British North

America Act are not modelled to the satisfaction of all. We know the Canadian government, our government, stands ready to study appropriate means of minimizing the present difficulties. Unfortunately, we cannot say the same for the Quebec government now.
My only reason for bringing up this subject today is to point out the necessity for close co-operation between the various elements of the country, and the danger of an individual being out of step and sabotaging the common effort towards the building of a strong and powerful nation. It is for that reason I limited my remarks on the constitution to general viewpoints without going into details, and emphasizing only that a false conception of the factual position of our constitution can become a menace to the future of national unity as well as to the welfare of a great portion of the population.
When we initiate a study to improve social welfare, particularly the rehabilitation of disabled persons and the establishment throughout the country of assistance to invalids, we find that if some increase could be brought about in these measures of assistance it would prove of tremendous relief to these people. In my province we already grant a measure of assistance to invalids.
There is one question that is of particular interest to me, sir, and that is the help and encouragement of the youth of this country. I feel that in Canada we have young people with talent, initiative and tremendous possibilities. Unfortunately many of them lack the means to put these potentialities to some use. With the eventual implementation of the Massey commission recommendations, why could we not devise some means whereby our young people could be given a helping hand and provided with an opportunity of serving the country in b manner more appropriate to their potentialities? I have seen many young people who were brilliant students and graduated from school with flying colours, yet they had to seek employment. If they were given the opportunity, these students would enter fields for which they feel they are better suited. If our young people felt there was a federal youth department to which they could apply for assistance or guidance, I am sure that before too long we would have the experts that today we are seeking from other lands.
A youth department established on a national scale would certainly not infringe upon the provincial departments of education. Through co-operation with the provincial departments we could have at the

disposal of our young people experts in the different fields of learning and craftsmanship who could give guidance to those young people who had not yet gone out on their own in life's struggle. These young people would be able to discuss their own problems and aspirations with men of experience. We certainly have fields or divisions in all departments of this government where such young people could serve. We could give guidance to the young men from the farm, who could study at experimental farms or stations throughout the country, as to new methods of farming that would improve the lot of those living on the homestead. Under the supervision of this new department young people in industry could learn for themselves, thus putting their own talents to the best use in order to make our world a better place in which to live.
The same thing might be said of the different fields of knowledge because with the proper guidance and the help of grants our young people could follow a course best suited to their aptitudes.

speechtext:
If we were to help the young men today I am sure it would pay dividends a hundredfold and give us better citizens tomorrow. I hope, sir, that before too long Canada will have a youth department, because it would pay countless dividends. If we are, even unwillingly, under obligation to spend billions to teach man to kill man, I believe the idea of a youth department is worth considering and some effort should be made to help our young people serve this country better.
On motion of Mr. Perron the debate was adjourned.

speechtext: Tomorrow we shall begin with the Department of Public Works. If it is completed tomorrow, we shall take the department of northern affairs for the balance of tomorrow. However, on Friday the minister of the northern affairs department will not be here, so we would go on with agriculture and national health and welfare.
